title: Grounding & Citations
summary: Retrieving the right chunks is only half of RAG; the model still has to answer from them and nowhere else. Grounding means injecting the retrieved chunks into the prompt with stable source ids, instructing the model to answer only from that context and cite the ids it used, and then verifying the answer's citations actually point at the supplied chunks. When no chunk supports an answer, a grounded system refuses rather than inventing one.

subtopics.title: Inject chunks with stable source ids
subtopics.explanation: You build the prompt by formatting each retrieved chunk with an explicit, stable identifier the model can point back to — a numbered tag like [1] or a source id. The id is the anchor for everything downstream: the model cites it, and your verifier resolves it. Without labeled sources in the prompt there is nothing concrete for a citation to reference, so id formatting is the foundation of the whole grounding contract.
subtopics.example:
def build_context(chunks):
    # each chunk gets a stable, model-visible id it can cite later
    blocks = []
    for i, ch in enumerate(chunks, start=1):
        blocks.append(f"[{i}] (source={ch['source']})\n{ch['text']}")
    return "\n\n".join(blocks)

context = build_context(retrieved)
print(context)
# [1] (source=refund_policy.md)
#     Refunds are issued within 5 business days...
# the number [1] is the anchor a citation will point back to

subtopics.title: Instruct the model to answer only from context and cite
subtopics.explanation: The system prompt sets the contract: answer using only the provided context, attach the bracketed id after each claim, and say you don't know if the context doesn't cover it. Explicit, repeated instruction plus a worked format example does most of the grounding work before any verification runs. Prompting alone is not a guarantee, but a precise grounding instruction is the cheapest and first lever you pull.
subtopics.example:
SYSTEM = (
    "Answer the question using ONLY the numbered context below. "
    "After each claim, cite the source id in brackets like [2]. "
    "If the context does not contain the answer, reply exactly: "
    "'I don't have enough information to answer that.' Do not use outside knowledge."
)
messages = [
    {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM},
    {"role": "user", "content": f"Context:\n{context}\n\nQuestion: {question}"},
]
# the contract: cite ids, stay in-context, or refuse

subtopics.title: Verify that citations resolve to supplied chunks
subtopics.explanation: After generation you extract the cited ids from the answer and check every one against the set of ids you actually injected. A citation to an id you never supplied is a hallucinated reference and should fail verification. This resolve-the-citations step turns 'the model said it cited sources' into 'the sources it cited are real', which is the difference between a claim of grounding and verified grounding.
subtopics.example:
import re

def verify_citations(answer, valid_ids):
    cited = set(int(m) for m in re.findall(r"\[(\d+)\]", answer))
    unknown = cited - valid_ids          # cited but never supplied
    return {
        "cited": cited,
        "all_resolve": not unknown,
        "hallucinated_ids": sorted(unknown),
    }

result = verify_citations("Refunds take 5 days [1], up to 7 [9].", {1, 2, 3})
print(result)  # [9] was never supplied -> all_resolve False

subtopics.title: Refuse when no chunk supports the answer
subtopics.explanation: Grounding's most important behavior is the refusal: if retrieval returns nothing relevant, or the answer would need a citation that doesn't exist, the system must decline instead of confidently making something up. You enforce this with an empty-context guard before calling the model and a post-check that an answer carrying claims also carries valid citations. A RAG system that refuses cleanly is far safer than one that always answers.
subtopics.example:
def grounded_answer(question, chunks, llm):
    if not chunks:                       # nothing retrieved -> refuse up front
        return "I don't have enough information to answer that."
    context = build_context(chunks)
    answer = llm(build_messages(context, question))
    check = verify_citations(answer, valid_ids=set(range(1, len(chunks) + 1)))
    if not check["all_resolve"]:         # cited a phantom source -> don't trust it
        return "I don't have enough information to answer that."
    return answer

subtopics.title: Grounding vs raw generation
subtopics.explanation: A raw LLM call answers from parametric memory: fluent, but unattributable and prone to confident fabrication on niche or fresh questions. A grounded answer is tied to specific supplied passages you can show the user and audit later. The whole reason RAG is trusted in production is that grounding makes answers checkable — you can point at exactly which chunk each claim came from, which raw generation can never offer.
subtopics.example:
# raw: no sources, no way to audit
raw = llm([{"role": "user", "content": question}])

# grounded: every claim is traceable to a chunk you can display
grounded = grounded_answer(question, retrieved, llm)
# grounded answer -> 'Refunds take 5 business days [1].'
# you can render [1] as a clickable citation to refund_policy.md

foundations.overview: Grounding is the discipline that makes a RAG answer trustworthy: the model must answer from the retrieved context and attribute each claim to a specific source. It has three parts. First, injection — you format each retrieved chunk with a stable, model-visible id (a bracketed number or source id) and place them in the prompt. Second, instruction — the system prompt tells the model to use only that context, cite the id after every claim, and explicitly refuse when the context doesn't cover the question. Third, verification — after generation you parse the cited ids out of the answer and confirm each one resolves to a chunk you actually supplied, catching hallucinated references. Wrapping all of this is the refusal contract: if nothing relevant was retrieved, or the answer's citations don't check out, the system declines rather than fabricating. Grounding is what separates 'a chatbot that sounds authoritative' from 'a system whose every claim you can trace back to a source and audit' — the property that lets RAG be deployed where correctness matters.
foundations.formalDefinition: Grounding is the constraint that a generated answer be entailed by an explicitly supplied context set C = {(id, text)}, with each claim annotated by the id(s) it derives from. Citation verification checks that every id referenced in the answer is a member of C; an answer that makes claims without resolvable citations, or that is produced from an empty C, is refused.
foundations.whyItMatters: Retrieval finds the right passages, but a model can still answer from memory, blend sources, or fabricate — and a fluent wrong answer is more dangerous than an obvious one. Grounding and citation verification make answers auditable and enable clean refusal, which is the precondition for using RAG anywhere a wrong answer has real cost.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of an open-book exam with a strict proctor. The textbook pages are the injected chunks, each with a page number (the id). The rule is: answer only from these pages and write the page number next to every fact. The proctor (verifier) then checks that every page number you wrote actually exists in the book — and if a question isn't covered by any page, the honest answer is 'not in the material', not a guess.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Support and documentation assistants that show clickable source links, internal knowledge bots that must cite the policy they quoted, legal and medical RAG where every claim needs provenance, and any 'ask your docs' product where users expect to click through to the original passage.
foundations.performanceImpact: Grounding adds retrieved-context tokens to every prompt (the dominant input-cost driver) and a cheap post-generation regex/lookup for verification; the refusal path can actually save a full generation when context is empty. The main tuning levers are how many chunks you inject and how tightly you format them.
commonUseCases: Answering from a knowledge base with clickable citations
Policy/compliance bots that must quote and attribute a source
Refusing gracefully when the corpus lacks the answer
Auditing which passage produced each claim after the fact

commonMisconceptions.myth: If the answer sounds like it used the context, it's grounded.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Fluency isn't grounding. The model can paraphrase memory or cite an id you never supplied; you must parse citations and verify each one resolves to an injected chunk.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A good citation instruction is enough on its own.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Instruction lowers hallucination but never to zero. Production grounding pairs the instruction with verification of the cited ids and a refusal path for when they don't check out.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Grounding means the answer is factually correct.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Grounding means the answer is attributable to the supplied context. If the retrieved chunk is itself wrong or outdated, a faithfully grounded answer can still be wrong — grounding is about provenance, not ground truth.

codeLab.instructions: Implement grounded_answer(question, chunks, llm) that (1) returns the exact refusal string 'I don't have enough information to answer that.' when chunks is empty, (2) otherwise builds a numbered context (ids start at 1), calls llm(question) to get an answer string, (3) extracts the bracketed citation ids from the answer, and (4) returns the answer only if it cites at least one id AND every cited id is within the supplied range — otherwise returns the refusal string. solution.code:
import re

REFUSAL = "I don't have enough information to answer that."

def grounded_answer(question, chunks, llm):
    if not chunks:                          # nothing retrieved -> refuse
        return REFUSAL
    valid_ids = set(range(1, len(chunks) + 1))
    answer = llm(question)
    cited = {int(m) for m in re.findall(r"\[(\d+)\]", answer)}
    # must cite at least one id, and every cited id must be one we supplied
    if cited and cited.issubset(valid_ids):
        return answer
    return REFUSAL

codeLab.testHarness:
chunks = [{"source": "a.md", "text": "..."}, {"source": "b.md", "text": "..."}]

# valid citation within range -> answer returned
assert grounded_answer("q", chunks, lambda q: "Yes [2].") == "Yes [2]."

# citation to an id never supplied -> refusal
assert grounded_answer("q", chunks, lambda q: "Yes [5].") == REFUSAL

# no citation at all -> refusal
assert grounded_answer("q", chunks, lambda q: "Yes, definitely.") == REFUSAL

# empty context -> refusal without needing the llm
assert grounded_answer("q", [], lambda q: "Yes [1].") == REFUSAL

print("all tests passed")
hints: Guard the empty-chunks case first and return REFUSAL before you ever call llm.
re.findall(r"\[(\d+)\]", answer) pulls the numbers out of bracketed citations; wrap them in int().
Use set.issubset to check every cited id is valid, and separately require the cited set to be non-empty so an uncited answer also refuses.

checkpoints.explanation: The id is the anchor of the grounding contract: the model cites it after a claim, and your verifier checks that the cited id matches a chunk you actually supplied. Without labeled sources there's nothing concrete for a citation to point at.

theory.question: What does it mean to 'ground' a RAG answer, and what are its concrete steps?
theory.directAnswer: Grounding means the answer is derived from and attributable to explicitly supplied context, not the model's memory. Concretely: inject retrieved chunks into the prompt with stable ids, instruct the model to answer only from that context and cite the id after each claim (and refuse if the context doesn't cover it), then verify after generation that every cited id resolves to a chunk you actually supplied. If citations don't check out or nothing relevant was retrieved, refuse instead of answering.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A contract binding the generated answer to a specific, supplied set of source passages, with per-claim attribution.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: A fluent model will otherwise answer from parametric memory or blend sources, producing confident, unattributable, and sometimes fabricated claims — unacceptable where correctness and auditability matter.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Format chunks as [id] blocks, add a system instruction to use only that context and cite ids, generate, parse the cited ids, and confirm each is in the supplied set; empty context or unresolvable citations trigger a refusal.

theory.whyImportant: It's the property that makes RAG trustworthy and auditable — you can show the user exactly which passage each claim came from and decline cleanly when you can't.
theory.realWorldExample: A docs assistant answers 'Refunds take 5 business days [1]' and renders [1] as a clickable link to the refund policy; a verifier confirms [1] was one of the injected chunks before the answer is shown.

followUps.question: Does grounding guarantee the answer is correct?
followUps.answer: No — it guarantees attribution to the supplied context. If the retrieved chunk is itself wrong or stale, a faithfully grounded answer can still be wrong. Grounding is about provenance, not ground truth.

followUps.question: Why verify citations if you already instructed the model to cite?
followUps.answer: Instruction lowers but doesn't eliminate hallucinated or missing citations; verification turns a claim of grounding into checked grounding and enables a refusal path.

theory.question: How should a grounded RAG system behave when retrieval returns nothing relevant?
theory.directAnswer: It should refuse — return an explicit 'I don't have enough information to answer that' rather than answering from the model's own knowledge. You enforce this with an empty-context guard before the model call and a post-generation check that any answer making claims also carries citations that resolve to supplied chunks; if not, you refuse. A system that declines cleanly is far safer than one that always produces an answer.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: The refusal behavior of a grounded pipeline when the supplied context can't support an answer.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Without a refusal path, an empty or irrelevant retrieval falls back to parametric memory, which is exactly the unattributable, fabrication-prone behavior RAG exists to prevent.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Check for empty/low-relevance retrieval up front and short-circuit to a refusal string; after generation, verify the answer's citations resolve, and if they don't, replace the answer with the refusal.

theory.whyImportant: Graceful refusal is often the single most important safety property of a production RAG system — a wrong confident answer is more damaging than an honest 'I don't know'.
theory.realWorldExample: A compliance bot asked about a policy not in its corpus returns the refusal string instead of guessing, prompting the user to escalate to a human rather than acting on a fabricated rule.

followUps.question: How do you decide retrieval was 'irrelevant' rather than just sparse?
followUps.answer: Use a relevance threshold on first-stage scores or a reranker score, and refuse when the best candidate falls below it — tuned against an eval set to balance refusals against missed answers.

followUps.question: Isn't refusing too often a bad experience?
followUps.answer: Over-refusal is a real cost; you tune the threshold and improve retrieval so genuine answers aren't refused, but a calibrated refusal beats a confident fabrication where correctness matters.

scenario.question: Users report your RAG bot occasionally cites source '[7]' that doesn't exist and makes up plausible-sounding policy. How do you diagnose and fix it?
scenario.directAnswer: The symptom is ungrounded generation slipping through: the model is inventing citations and blending in parametric knowledge. Add citation verification — parse the cited ids and confirm each resolves to a supplied chunk — and treat any unresolved citation as a failed answer that triggers a refusal. Tighten the grounding instruction with a worked format and an explicit refusal clause, and add an empty/low-relevance-context guard. Log the rate of unresolved citations so the fix is measurable.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A grounding-enforcement gap where instruction alone was trusted without verification.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Prompting reduces but never eliminates hallucinated citations and memory-blending; without a verifier, those answers ship unchecked.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Extract bracketed ids, compare against the injected id set, and route any answer with unresolvable or missing citations to the refusal path; monitor the unresolved-citation rate to confirm the regression is closed.

scenario.whyImportant: It shows the practical difference between claimed and verified grounding and gives a measurable signal (unresolved-citation rate) to track the fix.
scenario.realWorldExample: A team added a regex citation check plus a refusal fallback; the phantom-citation complaints stopped, and the logged unresolved-citation rate dropped from 4% to near zero, with a small rise in honest refusals they accepted.

followUps.question: How do you stop the model from blending in outside knowledge in the first place?
followUps.answer: A firm 'use ONLY the context, do not use outside knowledge' instruction, low temperature, and a worked cite-or-refuse example — but always backed by verification, since prompting isn't a guarantee.

followUps.question: What if verification starts refusing too many valid answers?
followUps.answer: Inspect whether the model is citing correct chunks in a format your regex misses (e.g. [1,2] or (source=...)); align the citation format and parser before loosening the check.

coding.question: Write a function that extracts citation ids from an answer and returns the answer only if every cited id is valid and at least one id was cited; otherwise return a refusal string.
coding.thoughtProcess: I parse bracketed integer ids with a regex into a set, then apply two conditions: the set must be non-empty (an uncited claim isn't grounded) and every id must be in the supplied valid set (no phantom citations). Only when both hold do I return the answer; otherwise I return the refusal string. Using a set makes the subset check clean and dedupes repeated cites.
lineByLine: The regex \[(\d+)\] captures the integer inside each bracketed citation; the set comprehension dedupes and converts to ints.
`if cited` requires at least one citation — an answer that cites nothing is not grounded and refuses.
`cited.issubset(valid_ids)` requires every cited id to be one we actually supplied, catching phantom citations like [7].
When both conditions hold the original answer is returned unchanged; otherwise the fixed refusal string is returned.
The __main__ block demonstrates a valid cite, a phantom cite, and an uncited claim resolving to answer, refusal, refusal.
coding.timeComplexity: O(n) in the answer length for the regex scan plus O(k) for the subset check over k cited ids.
coding.spaceComplexity: O(k) for the set of cited ids.

followUps.question: How would you support multi-id citations like [1,2]?
followUps.answer: Broaden the regex to capture comma-separated groups, split on commas, and add each id to the cited set before the subset check.

followUps.question: How do you also guard the empty-context case?
followUps.answer: Before calling the model, if no chunks were retrieved, short-circuit to REFUSAL so you never spend a generation on an unanswerable query.

testCases.expected: I don't have enough information to answer that.
I don't have enough information to answer that.

keyTakeaways: Grounding = inject chunks with stable ids, instruct the model to answer only from them and cite the id, then verify the citations resolve.
The source id on each chunk is the anchor: the model cites it and your verifier checks it against the chunks you actually supplied.
Instruction reduces hallucination but isn't a guarantee — parse the cited ids and reject any answer with unresolvable or missing citations.
When retrieval returns nothing relevant (or citations don't check out), refuse with a clear message instead of answering from memory.
Grounding gives provenance, not ground truth: a faithfully grounded answer built on a wrong chunk is still wrong, so retrieval quality still matters.
